strengths: Impressive empirical performance on challenging benchmarks, achieving 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD dev and 89.75% on Spider test, outperforming prior 7B/14B open-source models and several closed-source commercial pipelines.

Well-structured multi-agent decomposition that separates the cognitive load of Text-to-SQL into specialized stages: reasoning-driven schema linking (Grounding), multi-turn interactive trajectory rollout with live execution feedback (Generation), and next-token verification (Validation).

Comprehensive experimental analysis and ablations, including systematic evaluations of individual agent contributions, varying interaction turn limits (T = 1, 5, 10), scaling candidate rollouts (Best-of-N), and benchmarking the generative verifier against LLM-as-a-judge and self-consistency baselines.
Thorough documentation of implementation details, including complete prompt templates and training hyperparameters in the appendix to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: The individual elements heavily adapt existing methods—multi-turn interactive RL builds upon SkyRL-SQL, task decomposition follows standard multi-agent Text-to-SQL setups, and the validation agent directly adopts the generative verifier paradigm (Zhang et al., 2025b). The primary contribution lies in system integration and tuning rather than new algorithmic principles.

Lack of inference efficiency and latency analysis: Generating N = 8 rollouts with up to 10 interactive database turns, followed by generative verification scoring, implies substantial compute, token consumption, and database load. The paper does not report execution latency, GPU runtime, or token overhead compared to single-turn or monolithic baselines.
Evaluation on BIRD is restricted to the development set; official test set results via the BIRD leaderboard/evaluation server are missing.

Minor presentation anomalies and typos: The abstract ends with an empty URL ('Our code is available at'); Table 14 has a typo ('Unkonwn'); and ambiguous model references appear without clarification (e.g., 'GPT-5' in Table 2 and 'GPT-4.1' in Figure 4 and Table 14).

strengths: Strong empirical performance: MARS-SQL achieves impressive execution accuracy on challenging benchmarks (77.84% on BIRD dev, 89.75% on Spider test, and 78.13% on Spider-DK), outperforming several larger open-source models and strong closed-source multi-agent baselines despite using a 7B parameter backbone.

Well-structured agentic workflow: Decomposing the complex Text-to-SQL pipeline into RL-based schema grounding, interactive multi-turn policy execution (ReAct loop with database feedback), and generative trajectory verification addresses the compounding errors typical of monolithic pipelines.

Comprehensive and informative ablations: The paper provides thorough ablation studies covering the contribution of each agent (Table 3), the interaction turn budget during training and inference (Figure 3 and Table 10), and comparisons among different verification/selection strategies (generative verifier vs. self-consistency vs. LLM-as-a-judge, Table 14).

Strong out-of-domain transfer: Training exclusively on the BIRD training dataset and obtaining state-of-the-art performance on Spider and Spider-DK demonstrates robust schema generalization without cross-dataset data leakage.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual novelty: The core building blocks heavily adapt existing paradigms—the interactive RL generation relies on the SkyRL framework, the grounding and generation policies are trained using standard GRPO, and the trajectory verification adapts the Generative Verifier framework (Zhang et al., 2025b). The contribution lies primarily in the system integration and engineering execution rather than fundamentally new algorithmic components.

Evaluation fairness and compute budget clarity: Table 2 compares MARS-SQL against other baselines, but MARS-SQL relies on test-time scaling (sampling N=8 rollouts followed by generative reranking). While the paper shows greedy accuracy (69.88% at T=10 in Table 10), it is not always clear whether baseline numbers in Table 2 reflect single-pass greedy decoding, pass@k, or equivalent compute/sample budgets.

Clarity and notation inconsistencies: In Section 3.3, Equation 5 references 'M stochastic reasoning rounds' for the validation score, which conflicts with the notation M used in Section 3.2 for the number of trajectory interaction turns. Furthermore, Table 12 does not include scratchpad reasoning for the verifier, leaving it ambiguous how the stochasticity across M rounds in Equation 5 is realized.

Minor errors and unverified baseline references: Table 2 lists 'GPT-5' as a base model and Table 14 lists 'LLM as a Judge (GPT-4.1) Unkonwn' [sic], which appear to be typos or informal model designations that need clarification and correction for scientific rigor.

strengths: Strong overall performance on standard benchmarks, reaching 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD dev and 89.75% on Spider test using an open-source 7B base model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct).

Principled integration of an interactive ReAct-style loop with reinforcement learning (GRPO), enabling the policy to leverage real execution feedback and error messages to perform multi-turn error recovery.

Comprehensive ablation studies that evaluate individual components (Grounder, Generator, and Verifier), the impact of varying interaction turn budgets, and comparisons against alternative candidate selection mechanisms such as Self-Consistency and LLM-as-a-Judge.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison regarding test-time compute: MARS-SQL's headline numbers (77.84% on BIRD dev) rely on an 8-candidate rollout reranked by a specialized Validation Agent (as detailed in Table 10 and Table 14). However, in Table 2, these numbers are directly compared against baseline models that operate in single-pass / greedy settings without matching the inference budget or sampling budget.

No analysis of inference overhead, latency, or token cost: The complete pipeline requires schema linking, up to 10 interaction turns with database execution per rollout, 8 parallel rollouts, and multi-round stochastic generative verification per trajectory. The paper provides no metrics on average token consumption, wall-clock latency, or database load, which are critical practical bottlenecks for interactive agentic workflows.

Lack of official hidden test set evaluation on BIRD: Results are presented only on the BIRD development set (1,534 examples). Given the known risks of data contamination and prompt overfitting on dev sets, validation on the official blind BIRD test benchmark is necessary to substantiate claims of a new state-of-the-art.

Discrepancies and unsupported claims in the turn-budget ablation: In Section 4.3.2, the authors state that 'increasing T from 1 to 10 consistently improves both Greedy and Best of 8 accuracy' and that 'model trained with T=10 significantly outperforms models trained with fewer turns across all inference settings.' However, Table 10 shows that for the final reranked accuracy ('Select(%)'), the model trained with T=5 evaluated at T=5 achieves 77.84%, whereas the model trained with T=10 evaluated at T=10 achieves only 77.57%, directly contradicting the claim.

Limited conceptual novelty: The core building blocks represent a combination of existing paradigms: ReAct-based tool usage, GRPO-based trajectory optimization adapted from SkyRL, and generative next-token verification adapted from Zhang et al. (2025b). The execution reward does not account for known Text-to-SQL false-positive pitfalls, such as accidental execution matches on empty result sets.

Presentation and formatting issues: Minor typos and oversights are present throughout the draft (e.g., 'taui' instead of $\tau_i$ in Section 3.2, 'baesd on' in Appendix B.1, and 'Unkonwn' in Table 14).

strengths: Impressive empirical performance: MARS-SQL achieves state-of-the-art execution accuracy on prominent Text-to-SQL benchmarks (77.84% on BIRD-dev and 89.75% on Spider-test), outperforming competitive closed-source multi-agent systems and larger open-source models.

Principled and trainable agentic formulation: Instead of relying purely on static multi-agent prompting or monolithic supervised fine-tuning, the framework trains specialized agent roles using RL (GRPO) for schema grounding and multi-turn interactive generation with live database feedback, complemented by a generative verifier.

Extensive and thorough ablation studies: The paper meticulously isolates the contributions of schema pruning, multi-turn RL reasoning, interaction turn limits (T), candidate generation counts (N), and different selection/verification mechanisms (e.g., Table 2, Table 3, Table 24, Table 32).

Comprehensive cost, latency, and scaling analysis: The authors provide detailed profiling of training time (~13 hours on 4x H800s), inference latency, token usage, VRAM consumption, normalized-budget evaluations, and comparisons against parameter-matched ensembles (Appendix E, F, G).

Convincing demonstration of learned error recovery: Qualitative case studies and interaction turn distribution statistics (Appendix H, I) demonstrate that the generation policy learns genuine semantic self-correction and query decomposition rather than superficial syntax fixing.
weaknesses: High inference latency and resource footprint: Achieving the headline performance requires generating 8 trajectories with multi-turn database executions followed by 8 verification evaluations, leading to an average latency of ~22 seconds per query and an aggregate system footprint of ~21B parameters across three checkpoints.

Practical deployment constraints with live execution: The framework relies heavily on executing intermediate candidate SQL queries on live database instances during inference; while standard for interactive agents, this introduces execution overheads, state isolation requirements, and potential security considerations (e.g., sandboxing read-only transactions) that should be discussed.
Minor presentation issues and typos: There are occasional minor typos throughout the text (e.g., 'baesd' on page 14, 'detaile in Appendix E' on page 5, 'Unkonwn' in Table 32 on page 31).

strengths: State-of-the-art empirical performance: The framework achieves impressive execution accuracy on challenging benchmarks, notably reaching 77.84% on BIRD-dev and 89.75% on Spider-test, outperforming strong proprietary models and existing open-source baselines without in-domain training on Spider.

Principled interactive RL formulation: Training the generation policy with multi-turn ReAct-style database interaction using GRPO directly addresses error recovery from real execution feedback, demonstrating that interactive policy training can discover semantic and syntactic correction capabilities beyond static prompting.

Rigorous ablation and component isolation: The paper thoroughly validates each architectural role (grounding, generation, validation), varying turn budgets (T=1, 5, 10), rollout counts, and candidate selection strategies against strong alternatives like Self-Consistency and LLM-as-a-Judge.

Comprehensive resource and deployment transparency: The authors provide detailed accounting of computational resources, including training time (~13 hours on 4x H800s), inference latency under normalized time budgets, token usage, VRAM considerations, and multi-task single-model scaling comparisons.
weaknesses: Reliance on BIRD development set rather than official hidden test set: The reported BIRD evaluations are conducted exclusively on the 1,534 development queries; submitting to the official hidden benchmark leaderboard would further confirm that no unintentional test-set overfitting occurred.

Composite novelty: The individual algorithmic components (GRPO, ReAct tool execution, generative verification next-token scoring) are established methodologies; the primary contribution lies in their integration and domain specialization for text-to-SQL.

Deployment and latency overhead: Running an interactive multi-agent pipeline with candidate rollouts (N=8) and verification (M=8) incurs an average latency of ~22 seconds per query and an aggregate footprint of ~21B parameters, which may limit real-time usability in production settings.

Minor typographical and referencing errors: There are several typographical slips throughout the manuscript and appendix (e.g., 'baesd' in Section B.1, referencing 'Appendix 26' instead of Appendix M in Section 3.1, and 'Unkonwn' in Table 32).

strengths: Strong empirical results across standard Text-to-SQL benchmarks, achieving 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev and 89.75% on Spider-test, outperforming existing open-source baselines and proprietary agentic pipelines while training exclusively on BIRD.

Effective integration of interactive reinforcement learning (GRPO) within a multi-turn ReAct loop, demonstrating that sparse execution feedback can effectively teach models to recover from schema errors and refine filtering logic without step-by-step human demonstrations.

Comprehensive experimental ablations and isolation studies, including dataset-wide controlled isolation (Table 3), interaction turn scaling (Figure 3, Table 24), and rigorous comparisons against single-model multi-task baselines and equal-parameter ensembles (Tables 18–20).
Thorough reporting of operational efficiency and deployment costs, transparently detailing end-to-end latency, token consumption, peak VRAM implications, and accuracy under normalized time budgets.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual novelty, as the framework largely combines existing building blocks—ReAct-style execution loops, GRPO policy optimization, and generative verifiers (reward modeling via next-token prediction)—tailored to the Text-to-SQL domain.

Substantial inference latency and computational footprint: executing G=8 rollouts across multi-turn database interactions alongside verification requires ~22.1 seconds per query and an inference footprint of ~21B total parameters across three models, which may limit real-time interactive usability.

Heuristic reward design in the Grounding Agent: the reward function in Section 3.1 introduces arbitrary piecewise constants (e.g., 0.5, 0.2, 0.1) without ablation or sensitivity analysis demonstrating their robustness to different database domains.
Minor presentation and formatting discrepancies (e.g., batch size inconsistency between Section B text and Table 4, typo 'Unkonwn' in Table 32, and minor typographical spacing issues in Table 1).
